title: Ten things and one
hook: given ten things, one is held back, and he loses faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth salok: the Giver, and the open palm. Your line was hold gifts loosely. Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi five does some arithmetic. Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

A birthday. Ten presents on the table, wrapped, every one chosen with care. The child opens nine, then ten, and then asks: where's the eleventh? The one I asked for? And suddenly the ten are forgotten. The afternoon is about the one that isn't there. Most of us laugh at that, and most of us have done it, at thirty, at fifty, about a job, a body, a year. Guru Arjan put that same arithmetic into Sukhmani, more than four hundred years ago, as plain as a sum.
screen: `TEN PRESENTS ON THE TABLE.` → `WHERE'S THE ELEVENTH?` → `A SCENE AS PLAIN AS A SUM.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: das basatoo lai paachhai paavai. He takes ten things and puts them behind him. Das is ten; basatoo, things, gifts. Paachhai paavai: puts them at his back, out of sight. Then: ek basat kaaran bikhot gavaavai. For the sake of one thing, he throws away his trust. One thing held back, and faith goes. Commentators read that last word in slightly different ways, losing faith, losing credit, being shown as faithless, but the picture doesn't change. Ten received, one withheld, and the ten disappear behind the one. Notice the numbers. Ten against one isn't close. It's not a story about someone treated unfairly. It's a story about attention. The one missing thing sits in front of the eyes, and the ten slip behind the back, still there, still given, just unseen. That's why this ashtpadi follows a salok about the Giver. The ingratitude it describes isn't loud or rude. It's quiet, and it's ordinary, and it happens by turning around. And this is where the week ends. Six days ago, the third ashtpadi asked for the Name and deeds to match. Then the fourth: remember who made you; the ungrateful guest; and the child calling out, You are mother and father, to You this prayer. Then the fifth: the Giver, the open palm, and now ten things and one. A week of the same lesson from three sides. The gifts were always there. The question is which way we're facing.
screen: `DAS BASATOO: TEN THINGS.` · `PUT BEHIND HIS BACK.` · `ONE HELD BACK, AND TRUST GOES.` · `THE TEN, STILL THERE, UNSEEN.` · then, large: `TEN GIVEN, ONE HELD BACK.`

segments.voice: The practice: count ten things you've been given. Use your fingers. Start small and real: the breath you're taking. Water that came out of a tap today. Someone who answered a message. Your eyes, reading this. A bed. Keep going until all ten fingers are folded. If a missing thing pushes in, the one you wanted and didn't get, notice it, and let it stand at the back for once. Then rest your two full hands in your lap, and breathe with them. The bell holds the time.
Ten things and one. Das basatoo: given ten, one held back, and the ten are put behind the back.
Your line: ten given, one held back. Today, when you catch yourself staring at the one, turn around once and look at the ten. Day four hundred fifty-five. A week, done.

screen: `DAY 455 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF GIFTS AND THE GIVER.` → `TOMORROW: IF HE TOOK THE TEN.`

howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza as part of Sukhmani Sahib, often daily; preachers in katha often use the ten-and-one picture to talk about gratitude.

original.note: Gurmukhi: das basatoo, ten things; the opening words of ashtpadi five's first stanza.

trapdoor: what you thought: the stanza scolds people for wanting things.
what it means: it's about attention: the one missing thing hides the ten given.
what a scholar hears: 'bikhot gavaavai' is glossed variously (loses faith, forfeits credit, is exposed as faithless); the image sits right after a salok naming God denhaar, the Giver.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
